problem: VLA policies such as RT-2 and OpenVLA need ground-truth action labels, which ties them to one embodiment and action space and blocks learning from action-free internet video. Earlier latent-action methods (Genie, LAPA, IGOR) reconstruct raw pixels, so their latent actions also encode task-irrelevant dynamics such as camera shake, other agents' motion and lighting or texture changes, and this hurts policy pretraining.
motivation: A generalist robot should reuse knowledge across embodiments (Franka, WidowX, wheeled navigation robots, human hands) and tasks (manipulation, navigation) without hand-aligning their action spaces. The authors observe two things. Predicting in DINOv2 feature space removes pixel-level nuisance. Conditioning on language during a first stage lets task-irrelevant dynamics be absorbed into a separate codebook. Together these yield a compact, embodiment-agnostic, task-centric action vocabulary that a VLM can plan in cheaply.
key_idea: Learn a discrete, language-disentangled, task-centric latent action space from cross-embodiment and human videos in DINOv2 feature space; pretrain a 7B VLM to autoregressively predict these latent action tokens; then attach a small visually-queried decoder that turns latent actions into each robot's native actions.
insight: Most of the gain comes from what the latent actions encode. On LIBERO with Ego4D-only pretraining, Genie-style all-change latents reach 82.3% average, task-irrelevant latents 56.5% (0.2% on LIBERO-Long), and task-centric latents 88.7%. Replacing OpenVLA-style autoregressive action-bin decoding with the attention-pooled chunk decoder lifts LIBERO average from 73.6% to 95.2%, of which +2.7 comes from using visual embeddings as the query (92.5% → 95.2%). Feeding back just one step of the model's own previous latent action (4 tokens) is a cheap history signal: R2R-CE oracle SR rises from 30.6 to 47.1 and LIBERO-Long from 88.1 to 92.0. A compressed 16^4 action space lets pretraining converge in 960 A100-hours versus OpenVLA's 21,500.
method: Latent action model (LAM): IDM encoder (spatial-temporal transformer with causal temporal mask plus learnable action tokens) and FDM decoder (spatial transformer). Operates on DINOv2 patch features of frame pairs (o_t, o_{t+k}) with k set per dataset to span about 1 s. Latents are quantized with a VQ-VAE codebook (N=4 tokens, |C|=16), and the objective is L2 reconstruction of DINOv2 features of o_{t+k}; the decoder sees no history frames.

Two-stage latent action decoupling: Stage 1 feeds T5 instruction embeddings to both encoder and decoder, so the quantized latents capture only task-irrelevant dynamics. Stage 2 freezes that codebook, adds a new task-centric codebook VQ_TC with its own tokens and no language input, and the decoder reconstructs from both.

Generalist policy pretraining: Prismatic-7B (SigLIP+DINOv2 fused encoder, projector, LLaMA-2-7B) with the vocabulary extended by |C| special ACT_i tokens, trained with next-latent-action cross-entropy. Pseudo-labels come from the LAM on an OXE subset, a GNM navigation subset (RECON, CoryHall, SACSoN) and Ego4D; action labels are discarded. Cost is 20k steps, batch 1024, 32 A100 for about 30 h (960 A100-hours).

Latent action decoding head (12.6M params): multi-head attention pooling compresses the visual embeddings to one token. That token plus a learned query attends over the latent-action embeddings from the last VLM layer, and a linear projection maps the result to action chunks of the target embodiment (chunk size 12 on the real robot, 10 Hz on an RTX 4090).
Post-training: LoRA fine-tuning (about 123M trainable params), end-to-end, with latent-token loss plus L1 loss on low-level actions.

History latent actions as CoT-style prompt: the LAM labels the previous step's latent action (4 tokens), which is appended to the instruction at each step except the first. This gives temporal context without multi-frame visual tokens.
Navigation adaptation: fine-tuned on R2R-CE train (10,819 samples), taking only the current single RGB frame plus historical latent action and predicting VLN-CE low-level actions.

setting.backbone: Prismatic-7B VLM (SigLIP + DINOv2 vision encoders, LLaMA-2-7B LLM), fully pretrained on latent actions then LoRA fine-tuned; plus 12.6M-param action decoder; separate latent action model (spatial-temporal transformers on DINOv2 features + T5 text encoder)
setting.training_data: Pretraining (action labels discarded): Open X-Embodiment single-arm subset (Fractal, Kuka, Bridge, BC-Z, FMB, etc.), GNM navigation subset (RECON, CoryHall, SACSoN) and Ego4D human videos (mixture in Table A-I); 'Bridge'-only and 'Human'-only variants also trained. Downstream: R2R-CE train (10,819 samples); LIBERO suites (10 tasks x 50 demos each); CALVIN ABC; Bridge-V2 for SimplerEnv; 20-80 teleoperated trajectories per real-world task.
setting.observation: Single current monocular RGB frame + language instruction + previous-step latent action tokens (R2R-CE: no depth or odometry, no history frames); manipulation: third-view RGB only (real robot adds proprioception)
setting.action_space: R2R-CE: VLN-CE low-level discrete actions decoded from latent actions; manipulation: continuous 7-DoF end-effector action chunks decoded from 4 latent tokens (codebook size 16)
setting.simulator: Habitat (VLN-CE R2R); also LIBERO, CALVIN, SimplerEnv for manipulation

numbers_note: R2R-CE navigation results for all methods are shown mainly in a bar figure (Fig. 'Oracle success rate on R2R in VLN-CE') that is not in the text. The only navigation metric is oracle success rate: no SR, SPL or NE. UniVLA's own numbers (47.1, and 30.6 without history) come from the text and the history ablation table. Baseline LLaVA-Nav (and apparently NaVid) numbers are taken from a 100-episode subset of val-unseen, while UniVLA is evaluated on all 1,839 episodes, so the comparison is not like-for-like. Data scalability (including the R2R trend) and data efficiency are reported only in figures. SimplerEnv shows an internal inconsistency: the table gives a 47.9% average, the text 42.7%.
results: On R2R-CE val-unseen with a single RGB frame, UniVLA reaches 47.1% oracle success. The paper reports this as 29.6 points above a fine-tuned OpenVLA and 33.1 above LLaVA-Nav, far above Seq2Seq/CMA (8.10%), and comparable to NaVid, which encodes the full video history. On manipulation it sets a new SOTA on LIBERO (95.2% avg vs OpenVLA 76.5%, MaIL 83.5%) and CALVIN ABC→D (avg len 3.80 vs RoboDual 3.66). On a real Piper arm it reaches 81.7% SR, beating LAPA by 36.7 points. It uses under 1/20 of OpenVLA's pretraining compute, and even Bridge-only or human-video-only pretraining beats OpenVLA.
limitations: Latent action granularity (about 1 s) and codebook size (16, 4 tokens) are fixed and may not suit all embodiments; evaluation is mostly single-arm manipulation.
Navigation evaluation is thin: only oracle success rate on R2R-CE with no SR/SPL, RGB-only baselines, and baseline numbers partly from a 100-episode subset.
Task-centric disentanglement relies on language annotations during LAM training; instruction granularity affects what counts as task-relevant.
